doc_description: SEC Form 10-K for Best Buy Co., Inc. (fiscal year ended January 28, 2017) detailing its omni-channel Domestic and International segments and footprint (including the Canada brand consolidation), principal risks, FY2017 results ($39.4B revenue, $1.85B operating income, 20.8% Domestic online comp growth), capital returns (dividends and sizable share repurchases), notable CRT/LCD litigation settlement proceeds, liquidity/debt and lease commitments, and audited governance/internal control disclosures.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC Form 10-K filing for Best Buy Co., Inc. (Commission file 1-9595), a Minnesota corporation headquartered in Richfield, MN; common stock listed on NYSE.
- Registrant status and compliance: well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; not a shell company; compliant with reporting and interactive data filing requirements; delinquent filer disclosure not contained; market value of non-affiliate equity approx. $7.8B as of July 29, 2016; 309,110,840 shares outstanding as of March 20, 2017.
- Documents incorporated by reference: portions of the 2017 Proxy Statement for Part III.
- Cautionary forward-looking statements under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, referencing Item 1A Risk Factors and noting no obligation to update.
- Table of contents outlines Parts I–IV, including Business, Risk Factors, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Market and Stockholder Matters, MD&A, Financial Statements, Controls and Procedures, Governance and Compensation items, and Exhibits.
- Business description:
  - Best Buy is a leading provider of technology products, services, and solutions across stores, online, mobile apps, and Geek Squad; operations in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
  - Two reportable segments: Domestic (U.S.) and International (Canada and Mexico), operating an omni-channel model.
  - Brands include Best Buy, bestbuy.com, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, Magnolia Home Theater, Pacific Kitchen and Home, Best Buy Express, and regional websites.
  - Canada brand consolidation (March 2015): Future Shop integrated into Best Buy, closing 66 stores and converting 65 to Best Buy.
- Operations:
  - Centralized U.S. management for merchandising, pricing, supply chain, e-commerce, marketing, labor deployment, and corporate support; standardized store procedures with local flexibility.
  - International store operations similar to Domestic.
- Merchandise and services categories:
  - Consumer Electronics; Computing and Mobile Phones; Entertainment; Appliances; Services (consultation, installation, protection plans, repair, support, classes); and Other (snacks, beverages, sundries).
- Distribution:
  - U.S. online orders fulfilled via store pickup or delivery from distribution centers or stores; ship-from-store capability; most merchandise shipped from manufacturers to distribution centers, with direct-to-store for certain releases.
  - Canada and Mexico use a similar model.
- Suppliers and inventory:
  - In fiscal 2017, top 20 suppliers represented ~77% of purchases; Apple, Samsung, Sony, HP, and LG comprised ~53%.
  - Generally no long-term vendor contracts; inventory managed via demand monitoring, receipt adjustments, vendor markdown/return agreements; global sourcing for exclusive-brand products.
- Store development:
  - Approximately 1,200 large-format and 400 small-format stores across segments at fiscal 2017 year-end.
  - Omni-channel advantages include ship-from-store and in-store pickup; vendor store-within-a-store concepts; ongoing space optimization, lease renegotiations, and selective openings/closures.
- Intellectual property:
  - Portfolio of trademarks and patents; notable marks include Best Buy, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, Magnolia, Insignia, Dynex, Rocketfish, Pacific Sales, Modal, Platinum, My Best Buy, and the Yellow Tag logo.
- Seasonality: Concentration of revenue and earnings in fiscal Q4 due to holiday shopping.
- Working capital: Funded by cash, equivalents, short-term investments, operating cash flows, and revolving credit facilities; needs increase ahead of holiday season.
- Competition: Multi-channel and online retailers, service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile carriers; focus on customer experience, price competitiveness, price matching, scale, vendor partnerships, and integrated assets; note on evolving sales tax dynamics for online operators.
- Environmental matters: Commitment to sustainability; goal to reduce carbon emissions by 45% by 2020 vs. 2009 baseline through operational efficiencies and renewable sourcing; reference to Corporate Responsibility & Sustainability Report.
- Employees: Approximately 125,000 full-time, part-time, and seasonal employees in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, and a sourcing office in China; positive employee relations and competitive benefits aligned with local practices.

structure.title: Business.
structure.heading: Item 1. Business.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: Best Buy Co., Inc., incorporated in Minnesota in 1966, is a leading omni-channel retailer of technology products, services, and solutions operating in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico through stores, websites, mobile apps, and Geek Squad.
- Segments and brands: Two reportable segments—Domestic (U.S.) and International (Canada, Mexico)—operating under brands including Best Buy, bestbuy.com, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, Magnolia, Pacific Sales, and others. In 2015, Canadian Future Shop operations were consolidated into the Best Buy brand, with significant store closures and conversions.
- Operations model: Centralized management of merchandising, pricing, procurement, supply chain, digital operations, marketing, and support functions; standardized store procedures with local flexibility; international operations similar to domestic.
- Offerings: Six revenue categories—Consumer Electronics; Computing and Mobile Phones; Entertainment; Appliances; Services (consultation, installation, protection, repair, tech support, etc.); and Other (sundries).
- Distribution: U.S. e-commerce fulfilled via store pickup, ship-from-store, and distribution centers; similar model in Canada and Mexico.
- Suppliers and inventory: Highly concentrated supplier base (top 20 account for ~77% of purchases; Apple, Samsung, Sony, HP, LG ~53%); generally no long-term vendor contracts; robust inventory management and vendor agreements; global sourcing for exclusive brands.
- Store footprint and strategy: ~1,200 large-format and ~400 small-format stores at FY2017 end; stores central to omni-channel strategy (ship-from-store, buy online/pick up in store); vendor shop-in-shops; ongoing space optimization and lease actions; Canadian brand consolidation reiterated.
- Intellectual property: Portfolio of trademarks and patents (e.g., Best Buy, Geek Squad, Insignia, Magnolia, My Best Buy, Yellow Tag logo) viewed as important marketing assets.
- Seasonality and working capital: Peak revenue and earnings in fiscal Q4 (holiday season); operations funded by cash, investments, operating cash flow, and revolving credit; seasonal inventory build before holidays.
- Competition: Intense competition from multi-channel retailers, e-commerce players, service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and carriers; price transparency, sales tax dynamics, delivery speed/cost expectations, and price-matching pressure margins; scale and service used as differentiators.
- Environmental commitments: Focus on reducing operational carbon emissions (45% reduction goal by 2020 vs. 2009 baseline) and promoting energy-efficient solutions; further details in Corporate Responsibility & Sustainability Report.
- Workforce: Approximately 125,000 employees across geographies, with competitive, locally appropriate benefits and generally good employee relations.
- Public disclosures and governance: SEC reporting and filings accessible via Best Buy’s investor website and SEC channels; governance documents (bylaws, code of ethics, committee charters) available online.
- Key risk factors highlighted: Revenue and margin pressure from strong competition, online shift and delivery expectations, price transparency, higher service-driven cost structure, and rapid technological change/product life cycles affecting demand.

structure.title: Risk Factors.
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
structure.summary:
- The excerpt is from Best Buy Co., Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10-K and covers “Available Information” and an extensive “Risk Factors” section.
- Available Information:
  - Best Buy is subject to Exchange Act reporting and makes its SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and amendments) available free on its investor website and via the SEC (including the Public Reference Room and sec.gov).
  - Corporate governance documents (articles, by-laws, Board governance principles, Code of Business Ethics, and Board committee charters for Audit; Compensation & Human Resources; Finance & Investment Policy; and Nominating, Corporate Governance & Public Policy) are posted online and available by request.

- Key Risk Factors (potentially affecting revenue, profitability, cash flows, liquidity, and market value):
  - Competitive pressures: intense competition from multichannel retailers, e-commerce, vendors/carriers selling direct; heightened price transparency; delivery speed/cost expectations; higher service-driven cost structure compressing margins.
  - Rapid tech change and shifting consumer preferences: shorter, less predictable product life cycles; category emergence/decline, cannibalization, launch-driven demand spikes, pricing deflation, and content availability—all risking inventory, access to in-demand product, and brand reputation.
  - Vendor and carrier dependence: concentration among top suppliers; limited long-term contracts; vendor leverage on terms, pricing, allocations, returns/warranties; carrier policy changes affecting mobile activations/commissions; international sourcing risks (trade, FX, logistics, instability).
  - Product safety/quality and recalls: legal/regulatory exposure, reputational damage, and revenue/profit impact.
  - Services strategy risks: labor costs, warranty variability, in-home/service liability, data access/security in services, third-party installer risks, and challenges marketing services online.
  - Macroeconomic sensitivity: consumer confidence, inflation, employment, interest/tax rates, financing availability, housing, FX, and essential cost trends influencing demand and mix.
  - Supply chain vulnerabilities: dependence on vendors and third parties; capacity constraints, strikes/port issues, system disruptions, parcel carrier concentration, damage/loss, and excessive costs—heightened by e-commerce growth.
  - Talent attraction/retention: competitive labor markets, turnover, compensation pressures, and potential loss of key leaders affecting execution and profitability.
  - Brand reputation: social media amplification of customer feedback; potential declines in loyalty, service plan/gift card sales, employee engagement, and vendor relations.
  - Strategy execution: need to design and implement effective strategies in a dynamic market; risk of ineffective or poorly executed initiatives.
  - Real estate management: long-term leases, network optimization, format/location/layout decisions; potential closures, remodel costs, mismatched network, and lease expense burdens (including sublease risks).
  - Cost management: fixed/multi-year costs and higher service costs vs. competitors; need to drive efficiency to offset revenue volatility.
  - Liquidity and capital access: reliance on operations, cash, facilities, and vendor terms; risks from tighter vendor credit or constrained capital markets.
  - Credit ratings: current investment-grade ratings noted (S&P BBB-, Moody’s Baa1, Fitch BBB-; all Stable as of March 20, 2017); downgrades could raise borrowing costs and worsen terms.
  - Seasonality: heavy dependence on Q4 (holiday) for revenue and earnings; higher susceptibility to disruptions, intense promotions, and forecasting challenges.
  - M&A/joint ventures/alliances: integration, control, performance, and synergy risks; potential impairments and distraction of resources.
  - Data security and privacy: regulatory obligations; risks of breaches affecting employee/customer data, with potential litigation, penalties, higher security costs, and reputational harm.
  - Catastrophic events: natural disasters, epidemics, terrorism, civil unrest—causing operational interruptions and losses.
  - Exclusive brands (Insignia, Modal, Dynex, Init, Platinum, Rocketfish): added exposure to warranty/product liability, manufacturing/logistics disruptions, compliance, IP issues, and “conflict minerals” disclosures; importance of quality/availability/pricing to margins and loyalty.
  - Regulatory/legal environment: evolving requirements on environment, product safety/transport, data privacy/security, labor, corporate governance, escheatment, finance/tax, and trade policy (including potential border adjustment tax); litigation exposure and compliance costs.
  - Labor/employment changes: unionization rules, independent contractor laws, and wage/leave/scheduling mandates that could raise costs and affect service levels.
  - Promotional financing: reliance on third-party banks; program profitability exposed to transaction mix, promo terms, bad debt, rates, regulation, and competition; 23% of FY2017 revenue on branded cards.
  - IT systems dependence: criticality of MIS for operations; risks from failures, cyberattacks, traffic spikes, and outages on websites/mobile apps causing lost sales, higher costs, and reputational damage.
  - Third-party dependencies: IT, cloud, HR, loyalty, financing/credit cards, gift cards, warranties, support, transportation, insurance—disruptions could impair revenue and operations.
  - International operations (Canada, Mexico, and various legal entities abroad): added exposure to political/economic/legal/regulatory differences, trade/ownership rules, FX, cultural factors, IP enforcement, and remote oversight—potential for disruptions and impairments.
  - Forward-looking statements and guidance: failure to meet guidance or revised outlooks could lead to stock price declines.

- Item 1B (Unresolved Staff Comments): Not applicable.

- Income statement highlights: Revenue remained relatively stable around $39–41 billion; operating income improved to $1.85 billion in 2017 (operating margin 4.7% vs. 3.5% in 2016); net earnings from continuing operations rose to $1.21 billion in 2017 after weaker prior years (2013 showed a loss).

- Operating metrics: Comparable sales modestly positive in 2015–2017 (0.3–0.5%) after declines in 2013–2014; gross profit rate improved to 24.0% in 2017; SG&A rate around 19–20%; operating margin strengthened.
- Balance sheet and liquidity: Current ratio near 1.4–1.5; total assets about $13.9 billion in 2017; debt declined from $2.29 billion (2013) to $1.37 billion (2017); total equity $4.71 billion in 2017.
- Footprint: Continued rationalization of stores and space—total stores fell from 1,779 (2013–2014) to 1,575 (2017), with notable reduction internationally; retail square footage declined correspondingly.
- Notable item: 2017 results include $161 million ($100 million net of tax) from CRT and LCD litigation settlements, affecting net earnings; referenced to Note 12, Contingencies and Commitments.

- Introduces Item 7: MD&A, outlining its purpose and section structure: Overview; Business Strategy; Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue; Results of Operations; Liquidity and Capital Resources; Critical Accounting Estimates; New Accounting Pronouncements.
- Provides an Overview of the business: leading provider of technology products, services, and solutions across stores, Geek Squad, web, and mobile; operations in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico; two reportable segments (Domestic and International).

nodes.title: Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations.
nodes.heading: Item 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations.
nodes.start_phrase: Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations ("MD&A") is intended to provide a reader of our financial statements with a narrative from the perspective of our management on our financial condition, results of operations, liquidity and certain other factors that may affect our future results.
nodes.summary:
- Financial footnotes clarify items affecting operating income and net earnings:
  - Fiscal 2016 includes $201 million ($159 million net of tax) in restructuring charges.
  - Fiscal 2015 includes a $353 million discrete tax benefit from reorganizing certain European legal entities.
  - Fiscal 2014 includes $149 million ($95 million net of tax) in restructuring charges.
  - Fiscal 2013 (11-month, 48 weeks) includes $415 million ($268 million net of tax) in restructuring charges, $614 million (net of tax) in goodwill impairment primarily related to Best Buy Canada, and in discontinued operations $23 million (net of tax) in restructuring charges mainly for Best Buy Europe and $207 million (net of tax) in goodwill impairment related to Five Star.
- Comparable sales methodology:
  - Defined as revenue comparison from stores, websites, and call centers operating at least 14 full months; exclusions for relocations/remodels; acquisitions included after first full quarter post one-year anniversary.
  - Canadian brand consolidation (closure of 66 Future Shop stores, conversion of 65 to Best Buy, elimination of Future Shop website) led to removal of all Canadian store/website revenue from comparable sales from Q1 FY2016 through Q3 FY2017; International comparable metric paused and Consolidated comparable sales equaled Domestic. International comparable sales reporting resumed in Q4 FY2017.
- Definition of current ratio: total current assets divided by total current liabilities.
- MD&A purpose and structure:
  - Provides management’s narrative on financial condition, results, liquidity, and factors affecting future results.
  - Sections: Overview; Business Strategy; Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue; Results of Operations; Liquidity and Capital Resources; Critical Accounting Estimates; New Accounting Pronouncements.
  - To be read with the Consolidated Financial Statements and Notes (Item 8).
- Company overview highlights:
  - Best Buy is a provider of technology products, services, and solutions via stores, Geek Squad, websites, and mobile apps.
  - Operates in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico with two reportable segments: Domestic (U.S.) and International (outside the U.S.).
  - Fiscal year ends on the Saturday nearest the end of January; FY2015–FY2017 had 52 weeks; FY2018 will have 53 weeks with the extra week in Q4.

nodes.title: Overview
nodes.heading: Overview
nodes.start_phrase: We are a leading provider of technology products, services and solutions.
nodes.summary:
- Footnotes to selected financial data detailing significant non-recurring items:
  - Fiscal 2016: $201 million pre-tax ($159 million net) restructuring charges in continuing operations.
  - Fiscal 2015: $353 million discrete tax benefit from reorganizing European legal entities.
  - Fiscal 2014: $149 million pre-tax ($95 million net) restructuring charges in continuing operations.
  - Fiscal 2013 (11‑month, 48 weeks): $415 million pre-tax ($268 million net) restructuring charges in continuing operations; $614 million net goodwill impairment primarily related to Best Buy Canada; discontinued operations included $23 million net restructuring charges (primarily Best Buy Europe) and $207 million net goodwill impairment (Five Star). Notes clarify impacts on net earnings attributable to shareholders.
- Explanation of comparable sales methodology:
  - Compares revenue from stores, websites, and call centers operating at least 14 full months; excludes locations closed >14 days for remodel/relocation until 14 months post-reopen; acquisitions included starting first full quarter after one-year anniversary; excludes discontinued operations and, for International, foreign currency effects.
  - Canadian brand consolidation (closing 66 Future Shop stores, converting 65 to Best Buy, eliminating Future Shop website) removed all Canadian store and website revenue from comp base from Q1 FY2016 through Q3 FY2017, eliminating International comps; consolidated comps equaled Domestic during that period.
  - International comparable sales reporting resumed in Q4 FY2017; FY2017 International comps not provided because they would reflect only one quarter. Notes that comp-calculation methods vary across retailers.
- Definition of current ratio (total current assets divided by total current liabilities).
- MD&A structure and purpose:
  - Provides management’s perspective on financial condition, results of operations, liquidity, and factors affecting future results.
  - Sections: Overview; Business Strategy; Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue; Results of Operations; Liquidity and Capital Resources; Critical Accounting Estimates; New Accounting Pronouncements. To be read with Item 8 financial statements and notes.
- Company overview and reporting segments:
  - Best Buy is a provider of technology products, services, and solutions via stores, Geek Squad, websites, and mobile apps; operations in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
  - Two reportable segments: Domestic (U.S. and territories) and International (operations outside the U.S.).
- Fiscal calendar and seasonality:
  - Fiscal year ends on the Saturday nearest end of January; FY2017–2015 each had 52 weeks; FY2018 will have 53 weeks (extra week in Q4).
  - Business is seasonal with disproportionate revenue and earnings in Q4 (holiday period).
  - Reminder that fiscal 2013 was an 11‑month (48‑week) period.
- Non-GAAP financial measures:
  - Use and rationale for constant currency, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP effective tax rate, non-GAAP net earnings from continuing operations, non-GAAP diluted EPS from continuing operations, and non-GAAP debt to EBITDAR ratio.
  - Typical adjustments include restructuring charges, goodwill and non-restructuring asset impairments, and investment gains/losses; other items may be excluded for clarity.
  - Emphasis that non-GAAP measures supplement, not replace, GAAP and may not be comparable across companies.
  - Explanation of constant currency methodology (translating current results at prior-period exchange rates) and why it’s useful given FX fluctuations and Canadian brand consolidation.
  - References to reconciliations for non-GAAP measures and to the Other Financial Measures section for debt to EBITDAR; management views debt to EBITDAR as an indicator of creditworthiness and capacity to service obligations and fund growth.

nodes.title: Non-GAAP Financial Measures
nodes.heading: Non-GAAP Financial Measures
nodes.start_phrase: This MD&A includes financial information prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States ("GAAP"), as well as certain adjusted or non-GAAP financial measures such as constant currency, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP effective tax rate, non-GAAP net earnings from continuing operations, non-GAAP diluted earnings per share ("EPS") from continuing operations and non-GAAP debt to earnings before interest, income taxes, depreciation, amortization and rent ("EBITDAR") ratio.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights seasonality, noting a disproportionate share of revenue and earnings occurs in fiscal Q4 due to the Holiday period.
- Defines and details the methodology for comparable sales, including inclusion of stores, websites, and call centers operating at least 14 months; exclusions related to remodels/relocations, acquisitions timing, discontinued operations, and foreign currency effects; and cautions that methods vary across the retail industry.
- Explains the material impact of the Canadian brand consolidation (Future Shop closures/conversions and website elimination) on comparability: International comparable sales were suspended from Q1 FY2016 through Q3 FY2017, resumed in Q4 FY2017, and full-year FY2017 International comps are not provided to avoid misleading comparisons; consolidated comps aligned with Domestic during the suspension period.
- Outlines use of non-GAAP financial measures (constant currency, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP effective tax rate, non-GAAP net earnings and diluted EPS from continuing operations, and non-GAAP debt-to-EBITDAR), the typical adjustments (e.g., restructuring, impairments, investment gains/losses), their purpose for investors and internal management, limitations versus GAAP, and references to reconciliations.
- Describes the constant-currency approach and why it’s useful amid FX volatility and prior International comparability constraints.
- Discusses the non-GAAP debt-to-EBITDAR ratio as an indicator of creditworthiness and capacity to service obligations, and for comparability with retailers that own rather than lease stores; notes considerations in own-versus-lease decisions.
- Reviews FY2017 business strategy and progress against three priorities: strengthening the multi-channel core business, reducing costs/improving efficiency, and advancing growth/differentiation initiatives. Reported outcomes include market share gains despite a slightly declining market, a >350 bps increase in NPS, Domestic online comparable sales growth of 20.8%, International operating income improvement to $90M from a $210M loss (driven by Canadian consolidation), $350M cumulative cost savings toward a $400M three-year target enabling investment with near-flat SG&A, and testing new customer experience concepts.
- Introduces “Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue,” following completion of “Renew Blue,” with a customer-centric mission to be a trusted adviser/solutions provider and the home technology services source; aims for gradual revenue growth, ongoing cost savings, and more recurring, stickier revenue streams.
- Presents three growth pillars: maximize the multi-channel retail business (enhanced customer experience and key category investments), expand services and solutions (e.g., tech support, security monitoring, home automation), and accelerate growth in International (Canada and Mexico).
- Signals FY2018 priorities centered on driving growth from these pillars, including continued digital innovation to support the customer journey.

nodes.title: Business Strategy
nodes.heading: Business Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: During fiscal 2017, we executed against the three priorities we shared at the beginning of the year:
nodes.summary:
- Real estate strategy: Decisions to own vs. lease stores are based on liquidity, capital structure, preferences of both parties, and maximizing shareholder returns.
- Fiscal 2017 priorities and results:
  - Gained market share across most product categories despite an overall market decline in 2016.
  - Increased Net Promoter Score by over 350 basis points.
  - Domestic segment online comparable sales grew 20.8%.
  - International segment turnaround driven by Canadian brand consolidation, moving to $90M operating income from a $210M loss in fiscal 2016.
  - Achieved $350M of cumulative savings toward a $400M three-year cost reduction and gross profit optimization target, enabling customer experience investments while keeping SG&A near flat.
  - Explored and tested new customer experience concepts, with some planned launches in fiscal 2018.
- Strategic transition: Completion of the “Renew Blue” transformation and launch of “Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue,” centered on being customers’ trusted adviser and home technology services provider, and positioning as the leading technology expert simplifying discovery and enjoyment of tech.
- Financial aims: Gradual revenue growth, continuous cost savings to offset inflation and fund investments, and building more predictable, recurring revenue streams with stickier customer relationships.
- Three growth pillars:
  1) Maximize multi-channel retail by enhancing customer experience, investing in key product categories, and deepening relationships.
  2) Expand services and solutions (e.g., technical support, security monitoring, home automation) with associated products.
  3) Accelerate growth in International (Canada and Mexico).
- Fiscal 2018 priorities: Drive growth from these pillars, including continued innovation of digital capabilities to support the customer shopping journey.

nodes.title: Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue
nodes.heading: Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue
nodes.start_phrase: In November 2012, we introduced our transformation strategy called Renew Blue.
nodes.summary:
- Real estate strategy: Decisions to own or lease stores are based on liquidity, capital structure, owner preferences, and maximizing shareholder returns.
- FY2017 business priorities and outcomes:
  - Built on multi-channel strengths, drove existing business, reduced costs/boosted efficiencies, and advanced future-growth initiatives.
  - Gained market share despite a low single-digit market decline in 2016; Net Promoter Score up 350+ bps.
  - Domestic online comparable sales grew 20.8%.
  - International turnaround: Canadian brand consolidation drove $90M operating income vs. a $210M loss in FY2016.
  - Achieved $350M of a $400M three-year cost/GP optimization target, enabling customer-experience investments with near-flat SG&A.
  - Tested new customer experience concepts, with select launches planned for FY2018.
- Best Buy 2020: Building the New Blue (post-Renew Blue):
  - Customer-centric mission to be the trusted adviser/solution provider and home technology services partner, simplifying tech for customers.
  - Financial aims: gradual revenue growth, ongoing cost savings to offset inflation and fund investments, and more predictable, recurring, stickier revenue streams.
  - Three growth pillars:
    1) Maximize multi-channel retail via enhanced CX and focus on key categories.
    2) Expand services/solutions (technical support, security monitoring, home automation) with associated products.
    3) Accelerate growth in International (Canada and Mexico).
- FY2018 priorities:
  1) Drive growth through:
     - Digital capability innovation to support the shopping journey.
     - Focus on connected home, appliances, and improved mobile experience.
     - Expansion of the In-Home Advisor program.
     - Continued testing and scaling of new customer experience concepts.
     - International growth: online channel expansion, Canadian store remodels, and nine new stores in Mexico over two years.
  2) Improve execution in sales effectiveness, large-item and small-package supply chain, and services fulfillment.
  3) Continue cost reductions and efficiencies beyond the current $400M program (with $350M achieved).
  4) Build capabilities via investments in people and systems to support growth, execution, and efficiency.
- Results of operations/MD&A notes:
  - Mexico operations are consolidated with a one-month reporting lag; no lag-period events required acceleration during the periods presented.
  - Jiangsu Five Star (International segment) is reported as discontinued operations; unless stated, results refer to continuing operations.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.heading: Results of Operations
nodes.start_phrase: In order to align our fiscal reporting periods and comply with statutory filing requirements, we consolidate the financial results of our Mexico operations on a one-month lag.
nodes.summary:
- Strategic priorities:
  - Drive growth in key product categories, emphasizing connected home, appliances, and revitalizing mobile through better customer experiences.
  - Expand the In-Home Advisor (IHA) program to more markets to provide personalized, in-home technology consultations.
  - Pilot and scale new customer experience concepts, with some expected expansions in fiscal 2018.
  - Grow internationally by strengthening the online channel, extending successful store remodels in Canada, and opening nine new stores in Mexico over two years.
- Operational improvements:
  - Enhance sales effectiveness, large-item fulfillment, small-package delivery, and services fulfillment capabilities.
- Cost efficiency:
  - Continue cost reductions after achieving $350M of a $400M target; next phase of savings to be defined upon completion of the current program.
- Capability building:
  - Invest in people and systems to support growth, execution, and efficiency goals.
- Results of operations and reporting:
  - Mexico operations consolidated on a one-month reporting lag, with acceleration for significant events if needed.
  - Jiangsu Five Star results reported as discontinued operations; other discussions focus on continuing operations.
- Consolidated financial performance (FY2015–FY2017 highlights):
  - Revenue slightly declined ($40.3B in 2015 to $39.4B in 2017), while comparable sales grew modestly (0.3%–0.5%).
  - Gross profit increased and gross margin improved from 22.4% to 24.0%; SG&A rate roughly stable around 19%.
  - Operating income rose (3.5% to 4.7% of revenue); net earnings from continuing operations improved to $1.207B in 2017.
  - EPS from continuing operations increased to $3.74 in 2017; total diluted EPS $3.81.
  - Notes clarify comparable sales methodology due to Canadian brand consolidation and the impact/phase-out of installment billing adjustments.
  - Accounting note cautions comparability of gross profit and SG&A rates across retailers due to supply chain cost classifications.
- Cash flow and capital returns:
  - Operating cash flow increased to $2.5B in 2017 (from $1.3B in 2016); year-end cash and investments were $3.9B (vs. $3.3B).
  - Paid four regular dividends and one special dividend totaling $1.57 per share ($505M aggregate) in fiscal 2017.

nodes.title: Consolidated Results
nodes.heading: Consolidated Results
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents selected consolidated financial data for each of the past three fiscal years ($ in millions, except per share amounts):
nodes.summary:
- Presents consolidated financial performance for fiscal years 2017, 2016, and 2015, including revenue, comparable sales, gross profit, SG&A, restructuring charges, operating income, net earnings, and diluted EPS.
- Key three-year metrics:
  - Revenue: $39.4B (2017), $39.5B (2016), $40.3B (2015); declines of 0.3%, 2.0%, and 0.7%, respectively.
  - Comparable sales gains: 0.3% (2017), 0.5% (2016), 0.5% (2015); 2016 figure excluding installment billing estimated impact was -0.1%.
  - Gross profit and margin: $9.44B/24.0% (2017), $9.19B/23.3% (2016), $9.05B/22.4% (2015).
  - SG&A and rate: $7.55B/19.2% (2017), $7.62B/19.3% (2016), $7.59B/18.8% (2015).
  - Restructuring charges: $39M (2017), $198M (2016), $5M (2015).
  - Operating income and margin: $1.85B/4.7% (2017), $1.38B/3.5% (2016), $1.45B/3.6% (2015).
  - Net earnings from continuing operations: $1.21B (2017), $807M (2016), $1.25B (2015).
  - Diluted EPS: $3.81 total and $3.74 from continuing ops (2017); $2.56 total and $2.30 from continuing ops (2016); $3.49 total and $3.53 from continuing ops (2015).
  - Discontinued operations: modest gains in 2017 and 2016; small loss in 2015.
- Explanatory notes:
  - Comparable sales methodology adjusted due to Canadian brand consolidation; International segment excluded from comps until Q4 FY17; FY16 consolidated comps equal Domestic comps.
  - Installment billing in mobile increased revenue and cost of sales with little impact on gross profit dollars; the adjusted comp metric excluding installment billing discontinued in FY17 as mix stabilized.
  - Caution on comparability of gross profit and SG&A rates versus other retailers due to supply chain cost classification differences.
  - Discontinued operations include amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests.
- Liquidity and capital allocation:
  - Operating cash flow rose to $2.5B in FY17 from $1.3B in FY16.
  - Cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments were $3.9B at FY17 year-end vs. $3.3B at FY16 year-end.
  - FY17 dividends totaled $1.57 per share (including a special dividend), or $505M.
- FY17 vs. FY16 drivers:
  - Revenue decreased 0.3%: FX (-0.2%), non-comparable sales (-0.3%), comparable sales (+0.2%).
  - Gross profit rate up 70 bps: Domestic +50 bps; International +20 bps.
  - SG&A rate flat; restructuring charges fell to $39M from $198M (prior year primarily International).
  - Operating income up $479M; margin increased to 4.7% from 3.5%, driven by higher gross margin and lower restructuring.
- FY16 vs. FY15 drivers:
  - Revenue decreased 2.0%: FX (-1.3%), non-comparable sales (-1.1%), comparable sales (+0.4%).
  - Gross profit rate up 90 bps: Domestic +90 bps; International flat.
  - SG&A rate up 50 bps: Domestic +50 bps; International flat.
  - Restructuring charges rose to $198M from $5M, driven by International.
  - Operating income decreased $75M; margin down to 3.5% from 3.6%, with higher restructuring partially offset by CRT/LCD legal settlement proceeds.

nodes.title: Fiscal 2017 Results Compared With Fiscal 2016
nodes.heading: Fiscal 2017 Results Compared With Fiscal 2016
nodes.start_phrase: Consolidated revenue of $39.4 billion in fiscal 2017 decreased 0.3% compared to fiscal 2016.
nodes.summary:
- Year-over-year financial comparisons for fiscal 2017 vs. fiscal 2016 and fiscal 2016 vs. fiscal 2015, focusing on revenue, gross profit rate, SG&A, restructuring charges, and operating income/margins.
- Fiscal 2017 vs. 2016:
  - Consolidated revenue of $39.4 billion, down 0.3%, driven by FX (-0.2%), non-comparable sales (-0.3%), partially offset by comparable sales (+0.2%).
  - Gross profit rate up 70 bps (Domestic +50 bps, International +20 bps).
  - SG&A rate flat year over year in both segments.
  - SG&A restructuring charges fell to $39 million from $198 million (2017 primarily Domestic; 2016 primarily International).
  - Operating income increased by $479 million; operating margin rose to 4.7% from 3.5%, driven by better gross profit rate and lower restructuring.
- Fiscal 2016 vs. 2015:
  - Revenue decreased 2.0%, driven by FX (-1.3%) and non-comparable sales (-1.1%), partially offset by comparable sales (+0.4%).
  - Gross profit rate up 90 bps (Domestic +90 bps; International flat).
  - SG&A rate up 50 bps (Domestic +50 bps; International flat).
  - SG&A restructuring charges increased to $198 million from $5 million, driven by International.
  - Operating income decreased by $75 million; operating margin declined to 3.5% from 3.6%, primarily due to higher restructuring charges, partially offset by CRT/LCD legal settlement proceeds.
- Definition and treatment of non-comparable sales, including International segment timing, store openings/closings, and revenue streams excluded from comparable sales (profit share, certain credit card revenue, gift card breakage, and wholesale/dealer sales).
- References to a Segment Performance Summary for additional detail on gross profit and SG&A rate changes by segment.

nodes.title: Fiscal 2016 Results Compared With Fiscal 2015
nodes.heading: Fiscal 2016 Results Compared With Fiscal 2015
nodes.start_phrase: The components of the 2.0% revenue decrease in fiscal 2016 were as follows:
nodes.summary:
- Consolidated fiscal 2017 vs. 2016: revenue declined 0.3% to $39.4B; drivers were FX (-0.2 pts), non-comparable sales (-0.3 pts), partially offset by comparable sales (+0.2 pts). Gross profit rate rose 70 bps (Domestic +50 bps; International +20 bps). SG&A rate was flat. Restructuring charges fell to $39M from $198M. Operating income increased $479M, with margin up to 4.7% from 3.5%.
- Consolidated fiscal 2016 vs. 2015: revenue declined 2.0%, driven by FX (-1.3 pts) and non-comparable sales (-1.1 pts) offset by comparable sales (+0.4 pts). Gross profit rate rose 90 bps (Domestic +90 bps; International flat). SG&A rate increased 50 bps (Domestic +50 bps; International flat). Restructuring charges rose to $198M from $5M (International-driven). Operating income decreased $75M, margin down to 3.5% from 3.6%, partly offset by CRT/LCD legal settlement proceeds.
- Domestic segment performance (FY15–FY17): revenue roughly flat to slightly down in 2017 ($36.25B vs. $36.37B in 2016). Comparable sales grew 0.2% in 2017 (0.5% in 2016; 1.0% in 2015). Gross profit dollars and margin increased (to 23.9% in 2017). SG&A dollars slightly decreased with rate improvement (to 18.9% in 2017). Restructuring charges were $31M in 2017 (vs. $2M in 2016). Operating income rose to $1.76B (4.9% margin) in 2017.
- Digital/online: online revenue penetration increased to 13.4% of Domestic revenue in 2017 (11.0% in 2016; 9.8% in 2015); comparable online sales grew 20.8% in 2017.
- Installment billing: explains revenue/gross margin effects from mobile carrier installment plans; company discontinued the “ex-installment billing” comparable sales disclosure beginning in fiscal 2017 as mix stabilized.
- Store footprint: continued reduction in Domestic stores from 1,448 (FY15) to 1,363 (FY17), mainly from closures of Best Buy Mobile stand-alone locations and some core stores; notes ongoing lease evaluation.
- Domestic FY2017 revenue drivers vs. FY2016: comparable sales +0.2 pts; non-comparable sales -0.5 pts; net revenue decline 0.3%.

nodes.title: Fiscal 2017 Results Compared With Fiscal 2016

nodes.start_phrase: Domestic segment revenue of $36.2 billion in fiscal 2017 decreased 0.3% compared to the prior year.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Domestic segment performance summary for fiscal years 2015–2017, including selected financials, online metrics, category mix/comp sales, store count changes, and year-over-year analysis.
- Headline financials:
  - Revenue largely flat: $36.1B (2015), $36.4B (2016), $36.2B (2017); comparable sales up modestly (1.0% in 2015, 0.5% in 2016, 0.2% in 2017).
  - Gross profit dollars increased and margin expanded from 22.4% (2015) to 23.3% (2016) to 23.9% (2017).
  - SG&A roughly stable dollars; rate at 18.4% (2015), 19.0% (2016), 18.9% (2017).
  - Operating income improved: $1.44B (2015), $1.59B (2016), $1.76B (2017); margin rose from 4.0% to 4.4% to 4.9%.
  - Restructuring charges: minimal in 2015–2016; $31M in 2017 tied to Renew Blue Phase 2.
- Online performance:
  - Online revenue as % of Domestic revenue rose from 9.8% (2015) to 11.0% (2016) to 13.4% (2017).
  - Comparable online sales growth: 16.7% (2015), 13.5% (2016), 20.8% (2017), driven by higher traffic and conversion.
- Installment billing:
  - Began offering carrier installment plans in 2015; increases revenue and cost of sales while leaving gross profit dollars relatively unchanged.
  - Comparable sales excluding installment billing reported in 2015–2016; discontinued in 2017 as mix normalized YoY.
- Store footprint:

- Profit-share revenue from extended protection plans:
  - Recognized $148M in 2016 (unusually strong), $110M in 2017; equal uplift to gross profit and operating income.
  - Decline in 2017 driven by lower premiums paid to underwriter; further declines expected.
- Fiscal 2017 vs. 2016:
  - Revenue down 0.3% (comps +0.2%, non-comps -0.5%).
  - Online penetration increased to 13.4%.
  - Category comp sales: Consumer Electronics up; Appliances up; Computing & Mobile Phones down; Entertainment down; Services down (lower reimbursement revenue tied to plan design changes and operational improvements).
  - Gross margin rate up on computing hardware margin improvements and higher CRT legal settlements, partially offset by lower mobile phone margins and reduced profit-share.
  - SG&A rate slightly lower due to cost reductions and lower incentives, partially offset by growth investments.
  - Operating income up $179M; margin improved to 4.9%.

  - Strong profit-share revenue ($148M) due to plan design changes, repair/fulfillment improvements, and favorable industry trends; accompanied by lower repair revenues for insurers.

nodes.title: Fiscal 2016 Results Compared With Fiscal 2015
nodes.heading: Fiscal 2016 Results Compared With Fiscal 2015
nodes.start_phrase: Domestic segment revenue of $36.4 billion in fiscal 2016 increased 0.9% compared to the prior year.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Best Buy’s Domestic segment performance and key drivers for fiscal 2017 vs. 2016 and fiscal 2016 vs. 2015, plus a Canada restructuring in the International segment.
- Domestic restructuring:
  - Fiscal 2017: $31 million in restructuring charges tied to Renew Blue Phase 2 (began Q1 FY2017).
  - Fiscal 2016: $2 million in restructuring charges; FY2015: $4 million; immaterial impact on operating income rate. See Note 4.
- Domestic operating income:
  - FY2017 vs. FY2016: Up $179 million; operating income rate rose to 4.9% from 4.4%, driven by revenue growth, gross profit rate improvement, and lower SG&A rate.
  - FY2016 vs. FY2015: Up $148 million; operating income rate rose to 4.4% from 4.0%, supported by higher revenue/margins and $75 million net CRT/LCD litigation proceeds, partially offset by higher SG&A.
- Domestic revenue (FY2016 vs. FY2015):
  - Total: $36.4 billion, up 0.9%.
  - Drivers: Comparable sales +0.5% (including ~0.6% benefit from installment billing) and non-comparable sales +0.4%; profit-sharing revenue from the externally managed extended service plan portfolio of $148 million (similar amount also recognized in FY2017).
  - Online revenue: $4.0 billion, up 13.5% comparable; penetration rose to 11.0% from 9.8%.
  - Store changes: Net closures (primarily small-format Best Buy Mobile in Q4) had immaterial revenue impact.
- Domestic category mix and comparable sales (FY2016 vs. FY2015):
  - Consumer Electronics (32% mix): +4.7% comps, led by large-screen TVs, Magnolia Design Center expansion, and streaming devices; offset by declines in point-and-shoot cameras and smaller TVs.
  - Computing & Mobile Phones (46%): -2.6% comps due to industry tablet declines and lower mobile phone demand.
  - Entertainment (8%): -3.6% comps on music/movies and gaming hardware declines.
  - Appliances (8%): +15.4% comps, aided by major appliances growth and Pacific Kitchen & Home expansion.
  - Services (5%): -11.6% comps from lower repair revenue due to plan design changes, operational improvements, and industry trends.
- Domestic gross profit (FY2016 vs. FY2015):
  - Up $404 million (5.0%); excluding $88 million CRT/LCD litigation proceeds, up $316 million (3.9%). See Note 12.
  - Positive drivers: profit-share revenue; better rates in computing via disciplined promotions; favorable mix shift away from low-margin tablets; lower low-margin repair revenue; more higher-margin large-screen TVs; credit card portfolio benefits.
  - Offsets: lower appliance rates; lower rate in mobile (mix of higher-priced iconic phones); weaker margins in portable audio; reduced mix of higher-margin digital imaging; greater mix of lower-margin wearables; investments in services pricing.
- Domestic SG&A (FY2016 vs. FY2015):
  - Up $258 million (3.9%); SG&A rate rose to 19.0% from 18.4%.
  - Drivers: investments in growth initiatives, reclassification of more vendor funding to cost of goods sold, higher incentive compensation; partially offset by Renew Blue Phase 2 cost reductions.
- International segment (Canada restructuring, FY2016 Q1):
  - Consolidation of Future Shop and Best Buy under the Best Buy brand.
  - Actions: Permanently closed 66 Future Shop stores; converted 65 to Best Buy.
  - Costs: lease exit, tradename impairment, property/equipment impairments, employee termination benefits, inventory write-downs.

nodes.title: International Segment
nodes.heading: 2.5.2.2 International Segment
nodes.start_phrase: During the first quarter of fiscal 2016, we consolidated the Future Shop and Best Buy stores and websites in Canada under the Best Buy brand.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of category performance in the Domestic segment (comparable sales trends):
  - Consumer Electronics: +4.7%, led by large-screen TVs, Magnolia Design Center expansion, and more streaming devices; partially offset by declines in point-and-shoot cameras and small/mid-size TVs.
  - Computing & Mobile Phones: -2.6%, driven by industry declines in tablets and lower demand for mobile phones.
  - Entertainment: -3.6%, reflecting declines in music, movies, and gaming hardware.
  - Appliances: +15.4%, due to growth in major appliances and expansion of Pacific Kitchen & Home stores-within-a-store.
  - Services: -11.6%, from lower repair revenue on extended protection plan claims tied to plan design changes, operational improvements, and industry trends.

- Domestic segment profitability and costs:
  - Gross profit increased $404M (5.0%) year-over-year; excluding $88M CRT/LCD litigation settlement, up $316M (3.9%).
  - Gross profit rate improved due to: periodic profit-share revenue; better rates in computing hardware from disciplined promotions; mix shift away from low-margin tablets; lower low-margin repair revenue; higher mix of higher-margin large-screen TVs; and positive impact from the credit card portfolio.
  - Partially offset by: lower rates in large appliances; lower rate in mobile from higher-priced iconic phone mix; margin declines in portable audio; reduced mix of higher-margin digital imaging; higher mix of lower-margin wearables; and service pricing investments.
  - SG&A increased $258M (3.9%); SG&A rate rose to 19.0% from 18.4%, driven by growth investments, reclassification of more vendor funding to COGS, and higher incentive compensation; partially offset by Renew Blue Phase 2 cost reductions.
  - Restructuring charges were $2M in FY2016 (vs. $4M in FY2015), with immaterial impact on operating income rate.
  - Operating income increased $148M; operating income rate rose to 4.4% from 4.0%, helped by higher revenue/margin and $75M net CRT/LCD settlement proceeds, partially offset by higher SG&A.

- International segment restructuring and branding in Canada:
  - In Q1 FY2016, consolidation of Future Shop and Best Buy brands under Best Buy in Canada: 66 Future Shop stores closed; remaining 65 converted to Best Buy.
  - Related costs included lease exits, tradename impairment, PPE impairments, termination benefits, and inventory write-downs.

- International segment performance (FY2015–FY2017 highlights):
  - Revenue: $4,284M (2015) → $3,163M (2016) → $3,155M (2017); FY2017 down 0.3% vs. FY2016.
  - Gross profit and rate: $967M/22.6% (2015), $707M/22.4% (2016), $790M/25.0% (2017).
  - SG&A and rate: $953M/22.2% (2015), $721M/22.8% (2016), $692M/21.9% (2017).
  - Restructuring charges: minimal in 2015, significant in 2016 ($196M), $8M in 2017.
  - Operating income (loss): $13M (0.3%) in 2015; $(210)M (–6.6%) in 2016; $90M (2.9%) in 2017—strong recovery in 2017 post-restructuring.
  - Comparable sales metrics not provided for 2016–2017 due to Canadian brand consolidation impact; Q4 FY2017 international comps +0.9%.

- International store footprint changes:
  - Canada: Future Shop reduced from 133 to 0 through closures/conversions; Best Buy stores increased via conversions; Best Buy Mobile declined slightly.
  - Mexico: modest growth in Best Buy stores; slight reduction in Express.
  - Total international stores: 283 (FY2015) → 216 (FY2016) → 212 (FY2017).

- FY2017 vs. FY2016 International revenue drivers:
  - Non-comparable sales +1.8%; comparable sales +0.3%; foreign currency impact –2.4%; net revenue change –0.3%.

nodes.title: Fiscal 2017 Results Compared With Fiscal 2016
nodes.heading: 2.5.2.2.1 Fiscal 2017 Results Compared With Fiscal 2016
nodes.start_phrase: International segment revenue of $3.2 billion in fiscal 2017 decreased 0.3% compared to the prior year.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: International segment (Canada and Mexico) performance over fiscal years 2015–2017, including revenue, profitability, costs, store footprint, and effects of Canadian brand consolidation.
- Key financials:
  - Revenue: $4.28B (2015), $3.16B (2016), $3.16B (2017); YOY declines of 10.4%, 26.2%, and 0.3%, respectively.
  - Gross profit: $967M (2015), $707M (2016), $790M (2017); gross margin improved from 22.4% to 25.0% in 2017.
  - SG&A: $953M (2015), $721M (2016), $692M (2017); SG&A rate improved to 21.9% in 2017.
  - Operating income (loss): $13M (2015), $(210)M (2016), $90M (2017); operating margin moved from (6.6)% in 2016 to 2.9% in 2017.
  - Restructuring charges: $1M (2015), $199M (2016), $8M (2017); minimal COGS impact except $3M in 2016.
- Comparable sales: Withdawn for full FY2016–FY2017 due to Canadian brand consolidation; Q4 FY2017 international comparable sales +0.9%; FY2015 comps down 3.5%.
- Store portfolio changes:
  - Canada: Future Shop (133) closed/converted in 2015–2016; Best Buy units increased via conversion (136 at FY2016, 134 at FY2017); Best Buy Mobile declined to 53 by FY2017.
  - Mexico: Best Buy increased to 20 in FY2016; Express adjusted from 6 to 5 by FY2017.
  - Total international stores fell from 283 (FY2015) to 216 (FY2016) to 212 (FY2017).
- FY2017 vs FY2016 revenue drivers: Total -0.3% composed of +1.8% non-comparable sales, +0.3% comparable sales, and -2.4% FX impact.
- Revenue mix stable FY2017 vs FY2016: Computing & Mobile 48%, Consumer Electronics 31%, Entertainment 7% (down from 9%), Appliances 6% (up from 5%), Services 7% (up from 6%), Other 1%.
- Profitability drivers FY2017: Gross margin expansion from reduced prior-year promotional activity tied to consolidation and improvement in computing/home theater; SG&A rate leverage; sharply lower restructuring costs.
- FY2016 vs FY2015 decline drivers: -26.2% revenue due to store closures from Canadian brand consolidation, -12.5% FX impact, and softness in Canadian economy/CE industry; non-comparable sales -13.7%.
- Definition note: Non-comparable sales include net store activity (incl. consolidation), certain credit card revenue, gift card breakage, and wholesale/dealer sales.

nodes.title: Fiscal 2016 Results Compared With Fiscal 2015
nodes.heading: 2.5.2.2.2 Fiscal 2016 Results Compared With Fiscal 2015
nodes.start_phrase: In our International segment, revenue declined 26.2% to $3.2 billion in fiscal 2016 due to (1) the loss of revenue associated with closed stores as part of the Canadian brand consolidation; (2) a negative foreign currency impact of 12.5%; and (3) ongoing softness in the Canadian economy and consumer electronics industry.
nodes.summary:
- Presents International segment revenue mix by category for fiscal 2017 vs 2016 and for 2016 vs 2015, showing a largely unchanged mix (Computing & Mobile Phones ~48%, Consumer Electronics ~31%, Entertainment declining from 9% to 7%, Appliances and Services slightly rising). Notes that comparable sales data is not provided due to the Canadian brand consolidation.
- Fiscal 2017 vs 2016 (International segment):
  - Gross profit increased $83 million (11.7%); up $98 million excluding FX. Gross profit rate rose to 25.0% from 22.4%, driven by the non-recurrence of heavy promotional activity tied to the Canada brand consolidation and rate growth in computing and home theater.
  - SG&A decreased $29 million (4.0%); down $9 million excluding FX. SG&A rate improved to 21.9% from 22.8% due to sales leverage.
  - Restructuring charges were $8 million (vs. $199 million in fiscal 2016), related to adjustments of vacant space liabilities from the Canadian brand consolidation and the Renew Blue plan (changes in sublease income estimates).
  - Operating income improved to $90 million from a $210 million loss, driven by lower restructuring costs and better gross profit and SG&A rates.
- Fiscal 2016 vs 2015 (International segment):
  - Revenue declined 26.2% to $3.2 billion due to closed stores from the Canadian brand consolidation, a 12.5% negative FX impact, and softness in the Canadian economy and CE industry. Decrease components: FX (-12.5%) and non-comparable sales (-13.7%).
  - Gross profit declined $260 million (26.9%); down $141 million excluding FX. Gross profit rate slipped to 22.4% from 22.6% due to consolidation disruption and increased promotions in Canada.
  - SG&A decreased $232 million (24.3%); down $115 million excluding FX, reflecting cost elimination from closed stores, but SG&A rate increased to 22.8% from 22.2% on sales deleverage.
  - Restructuring charges totaled $199 million (vs. $1 million in 2015), primarily for Canada brand consolidation (facility closures, tradename and asset impairments, employee terminations).
  - Operating result deteriorated to a $210 million loss from $13 million income, driven by lower revenue, margin pressure, and restructuring, partially offset by lower SG&A.
- Additional consolidated results (Other income/expense):
  - Gains on sale of investments: $3 million (2017), $2 million (2016), $13 million (2015), from sales of cost-based investments.
  - Investment income and other: $31 million (2017) vs $13 million (2016) due to higher U.S. interest rates; $13 million (2016) vs $14 million (2015) reflecting lower Canadian rates and unfavorable FX translation.
  - Interest expense declined to $72 million (2017) from $80 million (2016) due to repayment of $350 million notes in March 2016; declined to $80 million (2016) from $90 million (2015) due to swapping some fixed-rate debt to lower floating rates. References provided to Notes on Restructuring Charges and Derivative Instruments.

- Focus areas: Income Tax Expense trends and Discontinued Operations.
- Income tax expense: $609 million (2017) vs. $503 million (2016) vs. $141 million (2015).
- Effective tax rate (ETR): 33.5% (2017) vs. 38.4% (2016) vs. 10.1% (2015); 2015 ETR would have been 35.6% excluding a $353 million discrete tax benefit from reorganizing certain European legal entities.
- Key drivers:
  - 2017: Higher pre-tax earnings increased tax expense; ETR decreased due to a higher mix of foreign pre-tax income and resolution of certain tax matters.
  - 2016 vs. 2015: Tax expense rose largely due to the absence of the 2015 discrete benefit and a lower mix of foreign earnings, partially offset by lower pre-tax earnings.
- Structural tax context: Consolidated ETR varies with jurisdictional rates; foreign earnings are generally taxed below the 35% U.S. federal rate, and are indefinitely reinvested outside the U.S., not subject to current U.S. tax.
- Discontinued operations (primarily Five Star in the International segment): 2017 gain of $21 million from sale of remaining property assets; 2016 gain of $90 million from the sale of Five Star; 2015 loss of $11 million due to other related charges.

nodes.title: Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.heading: 2.8 Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.start_phrase: Our consolidated financia l statements are prepared in accordance with GAAP.
nodes.summary:
- Off-balance-sheet arrangements and contractual obligations: Company has no off-balance-sheet financing other than operating leases. A contractual obligations table (as of January 28, 2017) totals $6.931 billion, covering long‑term debt, capital and financing leases, interest payments, operating leases, purchase obligations, unrecognized tax benefits, and deferred compensation, with payment timing by period.
- Key clarifications to the table:

  - Purchase obligations include binding agreements and open purchase orders (most fulfilled within 30 days); cancelable agreements are excluded.

  - Undrawn credit facilities of $1.25 billion could become short‑term debt if drawn.
- Critical accounting estimates (prepared under GAAP and reviewed with the Audit Committee; no material methodology changes noted):
  - Inventory valuation: lower of cost or market via markdown and inventory loss adjustments; significant judgment over demand, promotions, and obsolescence. A 10% change in markdowns would impact net earnings by ~$8 million.
  - Vendor allowances: generally recorded as cost offsets; receipt-based allowances deferred until sale; estimates require analysis of product/vendor mix and inventory turn. A 10% change in the deferral would impact net earnings by ~$23 million. Volume-based programs are accrued over the incentive period and adjusted if actual volumes differ.
  - Property and equipment impairments: recoverability testing when indicators arise, comparing carrying value to undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, impairment is measured to fair value (often via discounted cash flows). Impaired assets are rebaselined for depreciation. Assets are grouped at the lowest level of largely independent cash flows (store-level assets referenced).

nodes.title: Inventory
nodes.heading: 2.8.1 Inventory
nodes.start_phrase: We value our inventory at the lower of cost or market through the establishment of markdown and inventory loss adjustments.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from an Annual Report on Form 10-K discussing critical accounting estimates, referencing Note 1 (Summary of Significant Accounting Policies). Estimates involve significant judgment, are reviewed with the Audit Committee, and there were no material methodology changes noted.
- Inventory: Valued at the lower of cost or market via markdown and inventory loss adjustments; markdowns establish a new cost basis and are not reversed. Key judgments include consumer demand, promotional environment, and technological obsolescence. Sensitivity: a 10% change in markdown adjustment at January 28, 2017 would have impacted fiscal 2017 net earnings by approximately $8 million.
- Vendor allowances: Received through multiple programs and largely treated as offsets to product/service cost. Sell-through allowances recognized upon sale; receipt-based allowances deferred in inventory until sold. Estimation of deferrals is complex (product/vendor mix, inventory turns, program types). Sensitivity: a 10% difference in vendor funding deferral at January 28, 2017 would have impacted fiscal 2017 net earnings by approximately $23 million. Volume-based allowances are accrued over the incentive period based on expected purchases or sales, with limited year-end judgment due to program timing.
- Property and equipment impairments: Tested when indicators arise. Recoverability assessed via estimated undiscounted future cash flows; if not recoverable, impairment measured against estimated fair value (typically discounted cash flows). Recognized impairments reset the asset’s cost basis, which is then depreciated over the remaining useful life. Assets are grouped for testing at the lowest level of largely independent cash flows (e.g., store-level assets).

nodes.title: Vendor Allowances
nodes.heading: 2.8.2 Vendor Allowances
nodes.start_phrase: We receive allowanc es from certain vendors through a variety of programs and arrangements.
nodes.summary:
- Excerpt from a 10-K discussing critical accounting estimates, noting they require significant judgment, have been reviewed with the Audit Committee, and that no material methodology changes were made unless noted.
- Inventory valuation: carried at lower of cost or market via markdowns and inventory loss adjustments; markdowns set a new, nonreversible cost basis. Key uncertainties include consumer demand, the promotional environment, and technological obsolescence. Sensitivity: a 10% change in the markdown adjustment at January 28, 2017 would have affected fiscal 2017 net earnings by approximately $8 million.
- Vendor allowances: received under multiple programs and largely treated as reductions to product/service cost. 
  - Sell-through allowances are recognized as reductions to cost of sales when inventory is sold.
  - Receipt-based allowances are recognized upon receipt of inventory but deferred as a reduction of inventory until sale; the deferral estimate is complex (product/vendor mix, inventory turn, program types). The company does not expect material changes in these estimates. Sensitivity: a 10% difference in the vendor funding deferral at January 28, 2017 would have affected fiscal 2017 net earnings by approximately $23 million.
  - Volume-based allowances are accrued over the incentive period based on expected purchases or sales; adjustments may be needed if actual volumes differ, especially with tiered programs. Judgment at year-end is typically minimal because programs align with the calendar or fiscal year.
- Property and equipment impairment: assets are evaluated when indicators arise. Recoverability is first assessed using estimated undiscounted future cash flows; if not recoverable, impairment is measured by comparing carrying value to estimated fair value (typically using discounted cash flows). Recognized impairments reset the cost basis, which is then depreciated over the remaining useful life. Assets are grouped for testing at the lowest level with largely independent cash flows (e.g., store level).

nodes.title: Property and Equipment Impairments

nodes.summary:
- Overview of critical accounting estimates used in the company’s financial reporting, with methodologies largely unchanged and reviewed with the Board’s Audit Committee; references to detailed policies in Note 1 of Item 8 of the Form 10-K.
- Inventory valuation at the lower of cost or market via markdown and loss adjustments; no reversal of markdowns once recorded; significant judgment around demand, promotions, and obsolescence; sensitivity noted: a 10% change in markdowns at January 28, 2017 would impact fiscal 2017 net earnings by approximately $8 million.
- Vendor allowances accounting: most treated as reductions to product/service cost; sell-through recognized upon sale; receipt-based deferred in inventory until sold; complex deferral estimation driven by product/vendor mix, inventory turns, and program types; sensitivity noted: a 10% change in vendor funding deferral at January 28, 2017 would impact fiscal 2017 net earnings by approximately $23 million; volume-based programs accrued over incentive periods with adjustments if actual volumes differ.
- Property and equipment impairment testing when indicators arise: recoverability based on undiscounted cash flows; impairment measured using estimated fair value (typically discounted cash flows); assets grouped at the lowest independent cash-flow level (e.g., individual stores; shared assets evaluated across benefiting businesses); key assumptions include cash flows, useful lives, and discount rates.
- Goodwill impairment testing annually or upon triggering events at the reporting-unit level: Step 1 compares fair value to carrying value; if necessary, Step 2 derives implied goodwill; goodwill balance of $425 million at January 28, 2017, entirely in the Domestic segment, with substantial fair value headroom; acknowledgment of potential for material charges if outcomes diverge from assumptions.
- Tax contingencies: periodic audits by domestic and foreign authorities; liabilities recorded for uncertain tax positions and adjusted upon settlement, statute expiration, or new information; effective tax rate influenced by tax law changes, jurisdiction mix, earnings levels, and audit outcomes; potential for material impacts on earnings and cash from settlements.
- Across areas, emphasis on uncertainty, required management judgment, potential for material gains or losses if actual results differ, but belief that material changes to underlying estimates are not reasonably likely.

nodes.title: Goodwill
nodes.heading: 2.8.4 Goodwill
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill is not amortized but is evaluated for impairment annually in the fiscal fourth quarter or whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying value may not be recoverable.
nodes.summary:
- Impairment of property and equipment: The company reviews long-lived assets for impairment at the individual store level by comparing carrying values to store-specific net cash flow projections. Shared assets (e.g., distribution centers, IT) are assessed using aggregated cash flows of the businesses that use them. Impairment calculations rely on managerial assumptions about future cash flows, useful lives, and discount rates; while management does not anticipate material changes to these estimates, deviations could result in material impairments.

- Goodwill impairment: Goodwill is tested annually in the fiscal fourth quarter, or sooner if triggering events occur, at the reporting-unit level. Fair value is determined using discounted cash flows and market-based approaches. If fair value exceeds carrying value, no impairment is recorded; otherwise, a second step estimates implied goodwill via a hypothetical purchase price allocation to measure any loss. As of January 28, 2017, goodwill was $425 million, all within the Domestic segment, with fair value substantially exceeding carrying value. Management does not expect material changes in assumptions but acknowledges potential material charges if actual results differ.

- Tax contingencies and effective tax rate: The company’s tax returns are regularly audited by domestic and foreign authorities, with multiple years potentially open at any time. It records liabilities for uncertain tax positions (unrecognized tax benefits) and adjusts them upon settlement, expiration of statutes of limitation, or as new information emerges. Estimates involve significant judgment and uncertainty. The effective tax rate is influenced by tax law changes, jurisdictional mix of earnings (including new stores or ventures), profit levels, and audit outcomes. Results may be materially affected, with unfavorable settlements potentially increasing cash outflows and the effective tax rate.

nodes.title: Tax Contingencies
nodes.heading: 2.8.5 Tax Contingencies
nodes.start_phrase: Our income tax returns, lik e those of most companies, are periodically audited by domestic and foreign tax authorities.
nodes.summary:
- Property and equipment impairment: Store-level reviews compare carrying values to net cash flow projections; shared assets (e.g., distribution centers, IT) evaluated based on aggregate cash flows of utilizing businesses. Impairment calculations rely on management assumptions (cash flows, useful lives, discount rates); while material changes are not expected, deviations could trigger material impairments.
- Goodwill impairment: Tested annually or upon triggering events at the reporting-unit level. Step 1 compares fair value (DCF or market approaches) to carrying value; Step 2 (if needed) derives implied goodwill via a hypothetical purchase price allocation. As of January 28, 2017, goodwill was $425 million, all in the Domestic segment, with fair value substantially exceeding carrying value; estimates are not expected to change materially, but adverse outcomes could lead to material charges.
- Tax contingencies: Company is routinely audited by domestic and foreign tax authorities. Liabilities for unrecognized tax benefits are recorded and adjusted upon settlements, statute expirations, or new information. Effective tax rate is influenced by law changes, jurisdictional mix, earnings levels, and audit outcomes; favorable or unfavorable settlements can materially affect ETR and cash.
- Revenue recognition critical estimates:
  - Returns: Revenue recognized net of estimated returns at possession/service delivery; reserves based on historical data. A 10% change in the reserve at January 28, 2017 would affect net earnings by about $2 million.
  - Gift card breakage: Revenue recognized upon redemption; breakage recognized when redemption is remote and no remittance obligation exists, using historical patterns and recorded 24 months after issuance; estimates not expected to change materially but could be if results differ.
  - Customer loyalty programs: Points create a liability and reduce revenue based on projected redemptions from historical data. A 10% change in redemption rates at January 28, 2017 would affect net earnings by about $13 million. Overall, material estimate changes are not anticipated, but differences could be material.
- New accounting pronouncements: Referenced to Note 1, Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, in the consolidated financial statements.

- Market risk (Item 7A):

re sales when the customer receives and pays for merchandise.
