nodes.title: Credit card revenue
nodes.heading: Credit card revenue
nodes.start_phrase:
We offer promotional 
financing and credit cards issued by third-party banks that manage and directly extend credit to our customers.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency: Assets and liabilities translated at balance sheet date rates (one‑month lag applied where operations are reported on a lag); results and cash flows at average rates; translation adjustments recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income; transaction gains/losses recorded in SG&A and were not significant.
- Revenue recognition (general): Recognized when price is fixed/determinable, collectibility is reasonably assured, and the customer takes possession (or the service is provided); excludes sales taxes; reported net of estimated returns (based on historical rates), with a corresponding reduction to cost of sales. Sales returns reserve was $28 million (Jan 28, 2017) and $25 million (Jan 30, 2016). For multiple‑element arrangements, undelivered elements are deferred based on relative fair value (generally relative retail price).
- Deferred revenue: Primarily undelivered merchandise, incomplete services, and technical support contracts. Short‑term deferred revenue was $418 million (2017) and $357 million (2016); long‑term deferred revenue was $34 million (2017) and $45 million (2016).
- Merchandise revenue: In‑store sales recognized when the customer receives and pays for goods; ship‑to‑home recognized upon delivery; in‑store pickup recognized when customer takes possession; delivery fees recognized upon delivery.
- Services revenue: Consultation, design, installation, setup, repair, and classes recognized when complete. Extended warranty plans underwritten by third parties—company recognizes net commissions when related merchandise revenue is recognized; profit‑share recognized when the portfolio period ends and is estimable. Service/commission revenue from extended warranties was 2.2%, 2.3%, and 2.1% of revenue in fiscal 2017, 2016, and 2015; profit‑share revenues were $133 million, $158 million, and $19 million, respectively. Technical support contract revenue recognized straight‑line over the contract term or on a consumption basis when supported by history.
- Credit card programs: Promotional financing and credit cards issued and owned by third‑party banks; company holds no consumer receivables; profit‑share recognized when portfolio period ends and is estimable.
- Gift cards: Sold in stores, online, and via third parties; no fees or expiration. Revenue recognized on redemption or when breakage is probable and no escheat obligation exists; breakage recognized 24 months after issuance. Breakage income was $37 million (2017), $46 million (2016), and $19 million (2015).
- Sales incentives: Customer incentives (gift cards with purchase, coupons, rebates) reduce revenue at the time of sale based on expected redemption.
- Customer loyalty programs: Points recorded as a reduction of revenue and accrued liabilities when earned, based on projected redemptions; revenue recognized upon certificate redemption, expiration, or when breakage is likely; typical certificate expirations range from 2 to 12 months depending on membership level.
- Expense classification: Cost of goods sold includes product costs; inbound freight to distribution centers; vendor allowances not tied to specific, incremental, identifiable costs; cash discounts; service labor/benefits and parts freight; inventory losses; markdowns; customer shipping/handling; distribution network operating costs (payroll, occupancy, depreciation); and freight from distribution centers to stores.

nodes.title: Gift cards
nodes.heading: Gift cards
nodes.start_phrase:
We sell gift cards to ou
r customers in our retail stores, online and through select third parties.
nodes.summary:
- Promotional financing and co-branded credit cards: Credit is extended and accounts receivable are owned by third-party banks; the company holds no consumer receivables. Profit-share from banking partners is recognized as revenue after the portfolio period when amounts can be reliably estimated.
- Gift cards: Sold in stores, online, and via third parties; no fees or expiration. Revenue is recognized upon redemption or when breakage is deemed and no legal remittance obligation exists. Breakage is estimated from historical patterns and recognized 24 months after issuance; breakage income was $37M (2017), $46M (2016), $19M (2015).
- Sales incentives (coupons, rebates, gift cards with purchase): Treated as reductions of revenue at the time of sale based on expected redemption.
- Customer loyalty programs: Points earned reduce revenue and are recorded in accrued liabilities based on projected redemptions. Revenue is recognized when certificates are redeemed, expire, or are deemed unlikely to be redeemed (breakage), using historical redemption patterns.
- Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) components: Includes product costs; inbound freight to distribution centers; vendor allowances not tied to specific, incremental, identifiable costs; cash discounts; service-related payroll/benefits and parts with related freight; physical inventory losses; markdowns; customer shipping and handling; distribution network operating costs (payroll/benefits, occupancy, depreciation); and freight from distribution centers to retail stores.

nodes.title: Sales Incentives
nodes.heading: Sales Incentives
nodes.start_phrase:
We frequently offer sales ince
ntives that entitle our customers to receive a gift card at time of purchase or a reduction in the price of a product or service either at the point of sale or by subm
tting a claim for a refund (for example coupons, rebates, etc.).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of revenue recognition policies related to promotional financing, gift cards, sales incentives, and customer loyalty programs, plus classification of key cost components.
- Promotional financing and credit cards: Programs are issued and owned by third-party banks; the company holds no consumer receivables. Profit-sharing from banking partners is recognized as revenue when the portfolio period is complete and amounts are estimable.
- Gift cards: Sold in-store, online, and via select third parties; no fees or expiration. Revenue recognized upon redemption or when redemption is remote and no legal obligation exists (breakage). Breakage recognized 24 months after issuance and recorded in revenue. Reported breakage income: $37 million (2017), $46 million (2016), $19 million (2015).
- Sales incentives (e.g., coupons, rebates, gift cards at purchase): Recorded as a reduction of revenue at the time of sale based on expected redemptions.
- Customer loyalty programs: Points accrue a liability and reduce revenue when earned based on projected redemptions. Revenue recognized upon certificate redemption, expiration, or when redemption likelihood is low (breakage). Typical certificate expirations range from 2 to 12 months; breakage rates based on historical patterns.
- Cost classification: Details primary components of Cost of Goods Sold, including:
  - Product costs; freight from vendors to distribution centers; vendor allowances not tied to specific incremental costs; cash discounts.
  - Service costs (payroll/benefits for service employees; replacement parts and related freight).
  - Physical inventory losses, markdowns, customer shipping and handling.
  - Distribution network operating costs (payroll/benefits, occupancy, depreciation).
  - Freight from distribution centers to retail stores.

nodes.title: Customer Loyalty Programs
nodes.heading: Customer Loyalty Programs
nodes.start_phrase:
We have customer loyalty 
programs which allow members to earn points for each qualifying purchase.
nodes.summary:
- Describes revenue recognition for promotional financing and co-branded credit cards managed by third-party banks: the banks own the receivables; the company earns profit-share income recognized as revenue after the portfolio period is complete and the amount is estimable.
- Outlines gift card accounting: sold in stores, online, and via partners; no fees or expiration; revenue recognized upon redemption or when redemption is remote and no escheat obligation exists (breakage). Breakage is estimated from historical patterns and recognized 24 months after issuance; breakage income included in revenue ($37M in 2017, $46M in 2016, $19M in 2015).
- Explains treatment of sales incentives (e.g., coupons, rebates, promotional gift cards): recorded as a reduction of revenue at the time of sale based on expected redemptions.
- Details customer loyalty program accounting: points earn certificates redeemable at Best Buy stores; certificates typically expire 2–12 months from issuance. The retail value of points is recorded as a liability and reduction of revenue when earned, based on projected redemptions; revenue recognized upon redemption, expiration, or when redemption likelihood is low (certificate breakage), estimated from historical data.
- Lists primary Cost of Goods Sold components: product costs including inbound freight from vendors to distribution centers, certain vendor allowances, and cash discounts; service costs including payroll/benefits and replacement parts freight; inventory losses; markdowns; customer shipping and handling; distribution network operating costs (payroll/benefits, occupancy, depreciation); and outbound freight from distribution centers to retail stores.

nodes.title: Cost of Goods Sold and Selling, General and Administrative Expenses
nodes.heading: Cost of Goods Sold and Selling, General and Administrative Expenses
nodes.start_phrase:
The following table illust
rates the primary costs classified in each major expense category:

We receive allowanc
es from certain vendors through a variety of programs and arrangements intended to offset our costs of promoting and selling merchandiseinventories.

luded in SG&A, are expensed when the advertisement runs.

nodes.title: Stock-Based Compensation
nodes.heading: Stock-Based Compensation

We apply the fair valu
e recognition provisions of accounting guidance as they relate to our stock-based compensation, which requires us to recognize expense for the fair value of our sto
ck-based compensation awards.

nodes.title: Discontinued Operations
nodes.heading: 2. Discontinued Operations
nodes.start_phrase:
Discontinued operations are p
rimarily comprised of Jiangsu Five Star Appliance Co., Limited ("Five Star") within our International segment.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines what is included in SG&A: payroll and benefits; occupancy and maintenance; depreciation and amortization; advertising; vendor allowance reimbursements for specific promotional costs; tender and bank/interchange fees; charitable contributions; external service fees; long-lived asset impairments; and other admin costs (supplies, travel, lodging).

Notes related restructuring charges are discussed elsewhere.
- Defines fair value measurement policy: exit price framework, use of principal/most advantageous market, and a three-level hierarchy—Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (other observable inputs), Level 3 (significant unobservable inputs with management judgment). Emphasizes using the lowest-level significant input and the need for judgment for recurring fair value measurements.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.heading: 3. Fair Value Measurements
nodes.start_phrase:
Fair value is the price 
that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability (an exit price) in the principal or most advantageous market for the assetor liability in an orderly
 transaction between market participants on the measurement date.
nodes.summary:
- Summarizes aggregate results of all discontinued operations for fiscal years 2017, 2016, and 2015 (in millions), including revenue, restructuring charges, pretax gain/loss, income tax expense, gain on sale, and net earnings both including and attributable to noncontrolling interests.
- Key figures: revenue of $0 (2017), $217 (2016), $1,564 (2015); net earnings from discontinued operations attributable to Best Buy Co., Inc. shareholders of $21 (2017), $90 (2016), and $(13) (2015). References Note 4 for details on restructuring charges.
- Presents the company’s Fair Value Measurements policy (Section 3), defining fair value as an exit price in the principal or most advantageous market in an orderly transaction.
- Details the three-tier fair value hierarchy:
  - Level 1: unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical items.
  - Level 2: other observable inputs (e.g., quoted prices for similar items, quotes in non-active markets, and inputs corroborated by market data).
  - Level 3: significant unobservable inputs requiring management judgment.
- Explains that for recurring fair value measurements, observable data is used when available; when inputs span multiple levels, the measurement is based on the lowest-level significant input; and determining significance involves judgment specific to the asset or liability.

nodes.title: Assets and Liabilities that are Measured at Fair Value on a Recurring Basis
nodes.heading:
Assets and Liabilities that are M
easured at Fair Value on a Recurring Basis
nodes.start_phrase:
The fair value hiera
rchy requires the use of observable market data when available.
nodes.summary:
- Presents results of discontinued operations for fiscal 2017, 2016, and 2015, including revenue, restructuring charges, pretax gain/loss, income tax, gains on sale, and net earnings (including and attributable to Best Buy shareholders). Highlights: net earnings from discontinued operations attributable to shareholders were $21 million (2017), $90 million (2016), and $(13) million (2015). References Note 4 for restructuring details.
- Defines fair value and outlines the three-level fair value hierarchy (Level 1: quoted prices in active markets; Level 2: other observable inputs; Level 3: significant unobservable inputs).
- Details assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis as of January 28, 2017 and January 30, 2016, categorized by hierarchy level:
  - Assets include money market funds, commercial paper, time deposits, corporate bonds, foreign currency and interest rate derivatives, auction rate securities (ARS), and marketable securities funding deferred compensation.
  - Liabilities include foreign currency derivative instruments.
  - Notes no transfers between levels in 2017 and 2016; remaining ARS were called at par in 2017 (proceeds $2 million), leaving no Level 3 recurring items at year-end 2017.
- Explains valuation methods and key assumptions by instrument class:
  - Level 1: money market funds; mutual funds funding deferred compensation.
  - Level 2: commercial paper, time deposits, corporate bonds in non-active markets, foreign currency forwards/swaps, interest rate swaps (observable inputs like LIBOR, forward FX, and market quotes).
  - Level 3: ARS valued via discounted cash flow (DCF) using assumptions about future payments, benchmark rates, credit/guarantees, and liquidity risk.
- Describes nonrecurring fair value measurements for long-lived assets (fixed assets, goodwill, intangibles) when impaired, with charges recorded in operating income.
  - Summarizes impairments for continuing operations: $36 million in 2017 (primarily property and equipment) versus $131 million in 2016 (property and equipment and a tradename), with remaining carrying values approximating fair value.
  - Notes no nonrecurring fair value remeasurements related to discontinued operations in 2017 and 2016.
  - States all nonrecurring measurements used Level 3 inputs, typically via DCF of expected cash flows and appropriate discount rates; for restructuring-related assets, no future cash flows were assumed and sale values were nominal.
- Begins section on fair value of other financial instruments (cash, receivables, other investments, accounts payable, other payables, long-term debt); content is truncated.

nodes.title: Assets and Liabilities that are Measured at Fair Value on a Nonrecurring Basis
nodes.heading:
Assets and Liabilities that are M
easured at Fair Value on a Nonrecurring Basis
nodes.start_phrase:
Assets and liabilities th
at are measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis relate primarily to our tangible fixed assets, goodwill and other intangible assets, which are remeasured when the d
erived fair value is below carrying value on our Consolidated Balance Sheets.
nodes.summary:
- Explains fair value hierarchy classifications for financial instruments:
  - Interest rate swap derivatives measured using observable inputs (e.g., LIBOR) and classified as Level 2 due to being custom OTC contracts not traded in active markets.
  - Auction rate securities (ARS) classified as Level 3; valued via a discounted cash flow (DCF) model given lack of quoted prices and limited market information.
  - Marketable securities that fund deferred compensation are mutual funds classified as Level 1 based on readily available pricing.
- Details ARS DCF valuation assumptions: timing and amount of future interest and principal, forward interest rate benchmarks, probability of full principal repayment considering credit quality and guarantees, and investor required returns reflecting ARS liquidity risk.
- Describes assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis (primarily tangible fixed assets, goodwill, and other intangibles), with remeasurement only upon impairment and losses recognized in operating income.
- Summarizes impairment activity for continuing operations:
  - Fiscal 2017: total impairments of $36 million (property and equipment—non‑restructuring $28; restructuring-related property and equipment $8; no tradename impairment); remaining net carrying value approximates fair value.
  - Fiscal 2016: total impairments of $131 million (property and equipment—non‑restructuring $61 with $15 remaining net carrying value; restructuring-related property and equipment $30; tradename $40).
- Notes all nonrecurring fair value remeasurements used significant unobservable inputs (Level 3), with fixed asset fair values derived from DCF models using forecasts of revenues, expenses, significant cash outflows (e.g., capex), and appropriate discount rates; for restructuring-related assets, no future cash flows were assumed and expected sale values were nominal.
- Introduces a section on the fair value of other financial instruments (cash, receivables, other investments, accounts payable, other payables, and long-term debt).

nodes.title: Fair Value of Financial Instruments
nodes.heading: Fair Value of Financial Instruments
nodes.start_phrase:
Our financial instrumen
ts, other than those presented in the disclosures above, include cash, receivables, other investments, accounts payable, other payables and long-term debt.
nodes.summary:
- Fair value hierarchy and methodologies:
  - Interest rate swap derivatives measured at fair value using observable inputs (e.g., LIBOR) and classified as Level 2 (custom OTC, not actively traded).
  - Auction rate securities classified as Level 3; valued via a discounted cash flow model using assumptions about timing/amount of interest and principal, benchmark rate projections, credit quality/guarantees, and required returns given liquidity risk.
  - Marketable securities funding deferred compensation are mutual funds classified as Level 1 with readily available prices.
  - Other financial instruments (cash, receivables, payables) approximate carrying value due to short-term nature and would be Level 1 if measured at fair value; other cost-method investments approximate fair value; long-term debt fair value referenced in Note 5.

- Nonrecurring fair value measurements (impairments):
  - Applied to tangible fixed assets, goodwill, and other intangibles only upon impairment; reductions recorded in operating income.
  - No nonrecurring fair value remeasurements for discontinued operations in fiscal 2017 and 2016.
  - Continuing operations impairments (in millions): 2017 total $36 (property & equipment non-restructuring $28; restructuring-related property & equipment $8); 2016 total $131 (property & equipment non-restructuring $61; restructuring-related property & equipment $30; tradename $40). Remaining net carrying values approximate fair value and may reflect earlier measurement dates.
  - All nonrecurring measurements used significant unobservable inputs (Level 3) with DCF models based on forecasts of revenues, expenses, capital outflows, and discount rates; for restructuring-related assets, no future cash flows assumed and nominal sale values used.

- Restructuring charges (in millions):

nodes.title: Net Investment Hedges
nodes.heading: Net Investment Hedges
nodes.start_phrase:
We use foreign exchange fo
rward contracts to hedge against the effect of Canadian dollar exchange rate fluctuations on a portion of our net investment in our Canadian operations.
nodes.summary:
- The company uses derivatives solely for risk management of foreign currency and interest rate exposures, not for trading or speculation. It avoids credit-risk contingent features and uses investment-grade counterparties.
- All derivatives are recorded at fair value on the Consolidated Balance Sheet. Hedge effectiveness is assessed prospectively and retrospectively, and hedging relationships are formally documented at inception. The company also holds derivatives not designated as hedges.
- Net investment hedges: Foreign exchange forward contracts hedge Canadian dollar exposure on a portion of the company’s net investment in Canadian operations (terms up to 12 months). Fair value changes are recorded in other comprehensive income within foreign currency translation and reclassified to earnings only upon complete or substantially complete liquidation of the hedged investment; any ineffectiveness is recognized in earnings.
- Interest rate swaps: Receive-fixed, pay-variable swaps hedge portions of the 2018 and 2021 Notes.
